speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head U of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As an island nation, Singapore is vulnerable to the impact of climate change and the resulting more extreme weather conditions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have started on our transition to adopt more green practices to decarbonise.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Although Singapore accounts for only around 0.11% of the world's carbon emissions, we want to do our part as global citizens to mitigate climate change.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, as an international oil and gas refining, storage and trading hub, the transition while reducing our primary emissions to zero will not be easy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We will need to transform our economy and decouple growth from fossil fuel consumption.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To decarbonise our power grid, we have to increase solar energy provision and purchase renewable electricity from other countries such as through imports of renewable energy from the Lao PDR-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Being a small country without natural resources, regional cooperation projects like this with larger neighbouring countries which are endowed with big land masses suitable for harvesting solar, wind and hydroelectric are necessary.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Would the Ministry share what other regional cooperation projects are in the pipeline to boost our joint efforts to decarbonise as well as to manage and protect our regional environment and water resources?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are Singapore's capabilities and strengths which we can bring to the table in these collaborations to help in the fight against climate change?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How will the initiatives from the 28th meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP28) affect Singapore?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And how will the Government encourage stronger international cooperation to address climate change?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is well positioned to be the green finance hub for ASEAN and Asia.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We can also play an important role in transition finance to help companies become greener via long-term initiatives.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What can the Government do to encourage investment in climate action, especially in Southeast Asia?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Which are likely to be the most major changes that Singapore needs to prepare for?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the Government's plans in response to these projections?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Will some segments of our population be more vulnerable in the event of these weather changes and how can the Government support Singaporeans, especially those with less resources, in the green transition?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How will the Government increase public awareness of the implications of more extreme weather conditions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How can businesses, households and individuals play their part in the fight against climate change?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, with climate change, countries around the globe have been bracing themselves for changes in the nature of global supply chains and economic policy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One of the changes we have been following is the opening of the Northern Sea Route and how this may affect the economy of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The question at hand is not merely a transport or maritime issue which Minister Vivian Balakrishnan and Minister Chee Hong Tat addressed in 2020 and 2021 respectively, but is respectfully at heart an economic one.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, with climate change, should the Arctic sea ice continue with its current decline at a rate of 13% per year, an uninterrupted sea highway between Asia and Europe and the US that is navigable by large container ships will be created, allowing for a shorter route between Europe and the Pacific.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What this means is that cargo shipments may bypass the Suez Canal and the Malacca Strait, and hence Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This raises concern of whether Singapore will remain the top transhipment port in the world and a major port of call, which may in turn have trickle-down effects to the economy that should not be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would thus like to ask: one, whether the Government has an update on the climate developments of the Northern Sea Route since 2021; two, whether the Government has studied the possible economic impact of the Northern Sea Route to jobs and businesses in Singapore; three, has the Government studied the projected impact to the capacity of Tuas Mega Port in 2050 and beyond, should the Northern Sea Route become the predominant shipping route, and if so, whether it has taken any measures into account in the planning of the Tuas Terminals?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will our economic policy adapt to the changes brought about by the development of the route in the coming years?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And what are the Government's plans to ensure that the country remains economically competitive if the route should affect our status as a premier global hub, port and international maritime centre?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad the voices of activists were heard, and Singapore will raise our climate targets and achieve net zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is an ambitious target but one that is very much needed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government share whether we are on track to reach this target?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am also glad that Singapore is leading efforts to combat climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Part of these efforts include the Sustainability Action Package (SAP) for sharing expertise and best practices on sustainability and climate issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the SAP, Singapore will work with partners from the public and private sectors, and non-profit and international organisations to build capacity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government ensure that we cast a broad net and enable more diverse actors to contribute, including from smaller organisations and civil society groups who have valuable expertise to contribute?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this spirit, will the Government also look into increasing access research funding for a greater variety of researchers to join the research efforts and this global fight?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, in 2022, the Government raised our climate targets to achieve net zero emissions by 2050 as part of our Long-Term Low-Emissions Development Strategy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These new targets have been duly lodged UN Framework Convention on Climate Change in 2022.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is an ambitious undertaking given our constraints as an alternative energy-deprived city state.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I applaud the Government for pursuing these stretched targets and doing our part fight global climate change.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask for an update on the preparations and what steps is Singapore taking to achieve these targets?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, as a small island state, Singapore is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The fight against climate change demands unwavering commitment and bold actions.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As we navigate the path towards decarbonisation, I want to raise several key questions.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: First, how is Singapore keeping pace with emerging decarbonisation pathways?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We need to be actively exploring and investing in low- and zero-carbon technologies like renewable energy, hydrogen and carbon capture.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How can we ensure our efforts remain aligned with the latest advancements and evolving global strategies?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Second, how can we further engage the private sector and philanthropic organisations in supporting decarbonisation efforts?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What specific measures are being considered to mobilise private capital and expertise towards ambitious climate goals?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Third, how will Singapore catalyse green and transition finance, especially within Southeast Asia?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As a regional financial hub, we can play a leading role in channelling investments towards sustainable infrastructure, green projects and climate adaptation initiatives.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is a comprehensive strategy to develop green finance solutions and capabilities, promote green finance standards and disclosures, foster green finance innovation and collaboration and build green finance talent and awareness.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Investing in decarbonisation is not just an environmental responsibility.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is an economic opportunity for us as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: By embracing innovation, collaboration and regional leadership, Singapore can chart a course towards a greener, more resilient future for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Poh Li San and other Members have raised important issues which I will address from a whole-of-Government perspective.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Some of the details will be dealt with by the individual Ministries during their Committee of Supply (COS) debates.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I speak as Chairman of the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change (IMCCC).

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Amid heightened geopolitical and economic turbulence, the world is currently on a pathway to 2.1 to 2.8°C of global warming by 2100.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) has been working to improve our understanding of the consequences of such a pathway.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But it is a projection, because we are talking about what is going to happen for the rest of the century.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Third National Climate Change Study, released last month, forecasts the extreme climate conditions that we could experience – higher temperatures, heavier spells of rainfall, longer and more frequent dry spells.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This would be a marked increase from the historical average of 21 such days each year.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked how we are responding to these latest projections.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We take a long-term and proactive approach, and we are developing our adaptation plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These are regularly refreshed to keep up with the latest science, to help us be ready for the climate risks we will face – whether they are physical risks such as flooding, or health risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The physical effects of climate change also have wider implications for our economy, as Mr Dennis Tan has pointed out about the Northern Sea Route.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: If rising temperatures in the Arctic make this short-cut passable year-round, it could alter the flow of shipping between Asia and Europe.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our port will therefore have to be more efficient and better-connected to compete.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is why Singapore has been closely monitoring developments in the Arctic.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Although Singapore is on the equator, we have been an Arctic Council Observer State since 2013 – for the last 11 years – and we contribute and participate actively in its discussions.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Currently, the commercial viability of the Arctic routes remains low.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is a very difficult and treacherous route.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In 2022, only 43 transit voyages were made through the Northern Sea Route, fewer than the 85 transit voyages in 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Still, we cannot ignore how profoundly climate change can disrupt our lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For Singapore, this means not just acting now to achieve our own climate goals, but also catalysing regional and global action, so that other countries do the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Only then can we collectively achieve our global climate action goals.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Ms Poh Li San pointed out, we emit about 0.1% of the carbon dioxide each year, but we are affected by the other 99.9%.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have essentially decided to target for the future, look at what the future will bring for us, shape our economy and our society and plan on that basis rather than doing incremental changes as we go along.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how we are turning our ambitions into action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It shapes behaviour across our economy, and we continue to use the revenues to help businesses and households become greener.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I am truly heartened that both sides of this House have expressed support for a broad-based carbon tax.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Some have advocated, for example, from the Workers' Party (WP), much higher tax rates and sooner than what the Government is actually intending to implement up to 2030.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: What we are intending to implement is carefully calibrated to take into account the adjustment as needed by households and businesses and also the maturing of technologies that will make it more efficient for us to decarbonise.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are also transforming our energy mix to run on greener power.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have doubled our solar power deployment since 2021 to over 1,000 Megawatt-peak (MWp), despite our limited land area.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We aim to reach 2,000 MWp by 2030, or 2 Gigawatt-peak (GWp).

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As a comparison, our power supply consumption right now is about 8 GWp.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Of course, 2 GWp is not the same – you cannot put them side by side.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are importing low-carbon electricity, allowing us to tap renewable energy beyond our shores.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The FEF will allow us to plan ahead to catalyse the infrastructure investments we need to deploy low-carbon technologies, when they are viable.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There is a range of things it could be.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It could be hydrogen, could be ammonia, could be a number of things and we need to start doing that within the next few years.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are also looking at new solutions beyond the power sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have been monitoring carbon capture and storage (CCS).

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The technologies underpinning CCS are not new and there is growing recognition from countries and organisations, such as the International Energy Agency (IEA), that CCS can play an important role in achieving significant reductions of industrial emissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Countries in the region, such as Australia, Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia, have strong geological potential for carbon dioxide storage, and some of our regional partners have announced plans to develop as regional CCS hubs.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are ready to work with like-minded partners on pathfinder projects to catalyse the development of such regional hubs.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) will provide more details on this.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Chairman, the climate transition will take a whole-of-nation effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked how the Government is supporting businesses and households in this transition.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are benefiting from schemes that help them decarbonise and seize green economy prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: One example is bbp – an energy efficiency solutions provider.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Of course, developing a nice business for themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We will continue to enhance our schemes to encourage energy efficiency among businesses and households.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These include expanding the Energy Efficiency Grant to more sectors, enhancing the climate-friendly households programme that offsets the upfront costs of switching to more energy- and water-efficient appliances.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: MTI and MSE will update this House on their efforts in these areas in greater detail.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about support for our research community.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Government’s Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 Plan (RIE2025) allocates significant funding to R&D across every pillar of the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This ranges from low carbon energy research all the way to research in coastal protection and flood management, and covers a wide range of things.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We recently enhanced funding for the RIE2025 Plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This will facilitate the research community’s contribution to climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked how Singapore can play an active role in fostering international collaboration and catalysing global climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Chairman, domestic action alone is necessary but not sufficient for us to succeed in global climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: All countries and regions must do their part.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is why, under the Sustainability Action Package, Singapore supports capacity building for developing countries and brings together a diverse range of public and private sector partners to share best practices on sustainability and climate issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Minister Grace Fu helped broker a landmark consensus among the Parties to transition our energy systems away from fossil fuels.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is a strong signal of global resolve to pursue a net-zero future.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Beyond the negotiating rooms, the Singapore Pavilion at COP28 was a hive of activity.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It brought key organisations and persons from the private and people sectors together to forge new partnerships.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For example, Singaporean ocean carrier Pacific International Lines and Dubai-based port and terminal operator DP World signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to jointly develop green solutions to decarbonise global supply chains.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our Pavilion was also home to Singapore’s inaugural youth delegation to COP28.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our young people deserve our support to apply their energy and ideas to the challenge of climate change and make a real difference.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: MSE will share more about how the Government is enabling youth action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The world needs to continue the momentum from COP28 to accelerate climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked how Singapore can leverage our strengths as a hub to do that.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This substantial amount will need to be met by a combination of concessional and commercial capital.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As a financial hub, Singapore is well-placed to catalyse green and transition finance for the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore is also helping to build high-integrity carbon markets and pursuing collaboration on carbon credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement with various countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At COP28, we signed our first Implementation Agreement, and this was with Papua New Guinea.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: MTI will share more about our efforts on carbon markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore is helping to accelerate Southeast Asia’s energy transition by promoting partnerships that benefit our nation and the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Centre gives Southeast Asia greater access to the IEA’s expertise and facilitates capacity building.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As an aviation and maritime hub, Singapore can play a major role in developing the infrastructure and standards for green aviation and shipping.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) recently launched the Singapore Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint, which takes a balanced approach on the need for sustainability and competitiveness for our aviation sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This will help catalyse the development of sustainable aviation globally and facilitate the industry’s progress towards decarbonisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are also making progress on green shipping.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Singapore faces pressing demographic challenges such as an ageing population and a low birth rate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Life expectancy has also gone up and many choose to remain single.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Even those married may not have children either by choice or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Social issues such as ageism and increased caregiving responsibilities are further exacerbated by an uncertain global environment and economic outlook which present challenging conditions for Singapore’s economic growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Within this operating context, what are the key population outcomes that the Government wants to achieve for our future Singapore and what are the Government’s strategies to achieve these outcomes?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With fewer births and an ageing population, our local workforce is shrinking.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our NTUC strategy team recently embarked on a research study on our ageing population as well as slowing workforce growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We also expect to see a decline in job vacancies in manufacturing, construction and segments of the services sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We further submit that professional networks, flexible work arrangements (FWAs) and training opportunities and skills relevance foster their continued employment and facilitate their entry into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the study, we also found that there is a disconnect between perception and the actual action of hiring mature workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Implementing training plans for mature workers was perceived by employers to be the most effective in extending the career runway of mature workers but is unfortunately not among the top practices adopted.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My question is, therefore, how will we continue maintaining a vibrant economy that creates good job opportunities for Singaporeans and future generations amidst this slowing workforce growth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government elaborate on the key population outcomes envisioned for our future?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the Government's plans to achieve these outcomes within the current economic and demographic challenges?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Falling fertility is a challenge that developed economies are struggling with.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A shrinking workforce due to falling birth rates raises concerns about sustaining our economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will we continue maintaining a vibrant economy that creates good job opportunities for Singaporeans and future generations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This raises concerns about our long-term demographic sustainability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This trend aligns with other developed nations like South Korea, where despite significant investments in childcare subsidies, birth rates remain low.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What additional measures beyond existing schemes can alleviate concerns about starting and raising families?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While marriage and parenthood remain aspirational for many Singaporeans, factors like career goals and housing affordability can lead to postponed parenthood.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This delay, combined with the realities of biological limitations, can make achieving such aspirations more challenging.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Government to further support couples who want children and cultivate a national culture of proactive family planning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While awaiting the proposed extension of IVF co-funding to private clinics, what immediate options are available for couples actively seeking to start families?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can private clinics adequately address the affordability and quality concerns associated with fertility treatments?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In many developed nations, including Singapore, falling fertility has become a challenge.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fewer and later marriages, later and fewer births, a rapidly ageing population – these trends combined will have a significant impact on all aspects of our lives, our social fabric, workforce, economy, national defence and more.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will we be able to sustain our society and our standard of living?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Who will look after increasing numbers of elderly?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we continue to maintain a vibrant economy and create good jobs for Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even with advanced technology and artificial intelligence, manpower, especially younger people, are needed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What measures will the Government implement to reverse our falling fertility rate?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are we prepared to consider more extensive and innovative measures to support and encourage dating, marriages and procreation?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Accepting younger migrants and having more temporary foreign workers and employees in our workforce offer only a partial solution, as these measures come with their own challenges.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are also issues of social integration, cohesion and stability.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nonetheless, will the Government be reviewing immigration policies to counter our falling fertility rate?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, with 2030 only six years away and fast approaching, a key question arises – what are the Government's longer-term forecasts?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Population projections are a critical tool for public policy planning.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given current birth rates and the intake of new citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs), what are the Government's projections for Singapore's population in 2040 and 2050?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These figures are pivotal not just for immediate policy adjustments, but for securing a sustainable future for all.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government claims that it does not seek to achieve any particular population size.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If there is no population target, how does it decide how much to regulate the immigration tap or how much to invest in pro-natalist policies to achieve its desired economic, social and security outcomes over the long term?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Faisal Manap, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Set against the backdrop of an ageing population, these statistics become more worrying.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Following from that, I would like to ask for a progress update on the efforts to ensure that our infrastructure development is able to support an increasing population, in view of the delay and disruption in the construction sector resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is testament to the resilience and adaptability of our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But I also wonder if there are concerns of potential brain drain resulting from greater emigration.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Does the Government have a strategy of managing emigration to ensure Singapore itself does not lose out on our homegrown talent?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My final point is on the Government's effort in attracting Malay talent.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In the past years, me and a few other Malay Members of Parliament, including former President Mdm Halimah Yacob, had asked through Parliamentary Questions and COS cuts on the measures and efforts taken by the Government in attracting Malay talent.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Hence, I would like to ask for updates on the Government's efforts in attracting Malay talents till date.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As publicly known, there has been a Government stance in maintaining the racial balance in Singapore population to preserve social stability.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For example, does it make it more challenging for foreign spouses and/or family members of Singaporeans to be granted permanent residency, which is necessary before citizenship is considered?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to the Prime Minister's Office's (PMO's) clarification.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With the immigrant community already forming a significant share of the population, integration amongst all those who call Singapore home is crucial to keep our society cohesive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For this to happen, we need more social mixing and business networking, and these efforts should start from young.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: However, the vast majority of immigrant children attend international schools.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, perhaps including international schools in our national school games or forming joint sports teams between our schools and international schools is one way to bring Singaporean and immigrant students together, along with their parents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is the Government doing to support integration in schools, community and workplaces, and how can stakeholders across society do their part?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would the Government ensure that we can recruit and retain enough trained MDWs?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What will the Government do to encourage marriages and support young couples to have more babies?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many young people are working hard at their careers and further studies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Government assist and support them to network and meet potential marriage partners?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With these demographic challenges that we are facing as a nation, despite increasing Government financial incentives for young couples to start a family and have more children, I would like to ask: one, beyond the financial support, what other proactive and innovative approaches is the Government exploring to address the factors contributing to the decline in TFR?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I suggested setting up a social ecosystem of mentoring on family planning and financial management to alleviate the financial anxieties of setting up families in my Budget speech.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second question, considering the rising median age of first marriages and first-time citizen mothers, what additional measures can be taken to increase awareness of potential fertility challenges and encourage earlier family formation?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Seventy-two percent similarly think that it is not necessary to have children in a marriage, but most of them still would like to have children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our young people are increasingly focusing on furthering their education and career advancement over marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This aspiration and reality gap can contribute to continued implications on our demographic challenges.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, we need Flexible Work to be an imperative, as a country that needs to increase our total fertility rate – at the same time that people are coping with the rising demands of eldercare.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: One way to leapfrog this is to progress towards work-life integration, instead of getting stuck and caught with "work-life balance".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This goes beyond mere semantics to a fundamental shift in mindset and concept. "Balance" reinforces the idea that "work" and "life" oppose each other and that there is a need to cut back in order to achieve balance.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With the push for higher productivity amidst manpower shortages, "cutting back" of any sort makes companies nervous.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But with "Integration", the two are melded – potentially mutually enhancing each other.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Outdated notions like "going to work" or "clocking in and out" makes both employers and employees calculative when work encroaches into personal time or when personal matters encroach into work time.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such calculativeness is stressful and disempowering for both.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Life does not happen like clockwork, nor does business.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Work hours and routine helped organise people and shifts – which was relevant during the industrial era with factory-based work.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But now technology and communication tools allow many people to work anytime, anywhere.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We do business in the information and digital age, but we are still stuck in the industrial-era mindset when organising our workforce.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Integrating work and life allows for tasks in each domain to get done, whenever it can be done.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It enhances a sense of autonomy when employees can optimise their energies and time to organise their tasks in the most convenient and efficient manners that work for them.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These will help boost productivity and mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And that is how much people value such trust and autonomy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What are National Population and Talent Division's (NPTD)’s and Prime Minister's Office's (PMO)'s plans to accelerate work-life integration for a triple-win for employees, employers and Singapore?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Building a Singapore Made For Families requires a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many parents desire greater support and FWAs to better enable them to juggle work and family commitments.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For effective FWAs to happen, we need the support of employers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, reports show that post-COVID-19, companies have started to cut down on their FWAs offerings – citing productivity and trust issues.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For employers, FWAs must lead to productivity gains and a culture of trust must be created in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond providing for wider and extended family and elder-caregiving leave, I believe employers see FWAs as a tenable, sustainable way to retain and attract talent.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But our less resourced companies like our SMEs, may find it challenging to implement this on the ground in the same speed and scale as larger enterprises.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is therefore important to ask: how will the Government continue to support employers in building a more family-friendly environment for Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government's continued support for employers in implementing FWAs is critical in creating a family-friendly environment that meets the needs of our working caregivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together, we can build a Singapore that not only supports aspirations of our workforce but also nurtures strong and resilient families.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, this overlooks parents of children with severe disabilities or rare disorders who are undergoing care regardless of age.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The level of care for these children does not diminish and may even intensify as their condition progresses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As a result, many caregivers have appealed to their employers to use their personal medical leave instead; believing they would not need it for themselves due to their dedication to their child's well-being.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I brought up this issue during last year's Budget Debate, if the Government would consider extending childcare leave for parents of children with severe disabilities past the age of 12?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: What alternatives are available for these parents in terms of childcare leave?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A year later, unfortunately, we are still waiting for these two weeks of paternity leave to be mandated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The sad reality is that – as reported in the media – some companies are waiting for the paternity leave to be mandated before they give it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fathers are losing precious time with their babies – precious family time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We all wish this is not the case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We all hope that mindsets would have shifted, and paternity leave need not be made mandatory before companies give it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government must step in and ensure that we are indeed a Singapore made for families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our policies and our firm commitment can help shape mindsets and change them more quickly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, Prime Minister Lee urged couples to add a little dragon in this Year of the Dragon.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our record-low fertility rate is an existential problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have been generous in giving parents bonuses, vouchers and tax rebates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I hope we can give parents something even more valuable – time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every year, I know I sound like a broken record asking for more parental leave, more childcare leave, more parent care leave, fertility leave and annual leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But valuable time is important to many people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I sincerely hope the Government will consider providing parents with more parental leave – both maternity and paternity leave; and commit to a firm timeline to equalise both maternity and paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government also provide more incentives to companies to support them in giving their employees parental leave?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We support companies when it comes to giving their employees time to serve their reservist.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should provide the same level of support when it comes to giving their employees time to welcome their babies into this world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will help us truly become a Singapore made for families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, in a 2022 survey by the Breastfeeding Mothers Support Group Singapore, more than half of mothers stopped breastfeeding before their child turned one year old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The main reason cited was the challenges of expressing milk at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the rest of the offices, it is left to employers to provide lactation rooms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, there is an Accessibility Fund for building owners to upgrade their buildings or install a lactation pod.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government do more to publicise the Accessibility Fund and urge people to apply for it?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government also look into providing additional support for building owners to retrofit their buildings, with dedicated lactation rooms or install lactation pods?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, under the same Code, there must only be one – at least one lactation room – only at limited areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We recognise that our buildings should be inclusive in making sure that accessible toilets are widely available, even if some buildings may not have elderly or disabled users.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why the disparity when it comes to lactation rooms?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: About half of our population are female and many of them will go on to become mothers who should have the option of breastfeeding their children, if they wish to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We try to encourage Singaporeans to set up families through bonuses and vouchers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   The practice of "marrying first and then advancing your career" is not common in today's society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For many young couples, the pressure of raising children is very significant.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, they often hope to strengthen their respective career foundation, has stable financial capabilities before they consider whether or not to welcome a new life.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, by the time they reach that point, it is often too late.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When they wish to add more family members, they have already missed the last bus.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How should the Government alleviate the pressure on young couples to have more children and assist parents reduce and cope with their expenses and burdens of raising children?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How should the Government provide reassurances to Singaporeans, especially those in the lower, middle-income families to ensure that our children have a good starting point, regardless of the family's financial situation, especially in terms of their healthcare and early childhood education. : As the saying goes “it takes a village to raise a child”.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Hence, every bit of support – no matter how little – and be it through caregiving or financial assistance, is always a welcome relief to alleviate the stress encountered during parenthood journeys.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Not all couples are fortunate in the sense of having able-bodied parents, or being able to afford the cost of hiring a reliable helper to assist in caring for their young children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Based on the concerns that my Woodgrove residents have shared with me, these couples generally face greater concerns about caregiving arrangements – especially in the early stages of their child's life and even more so when they – the parents or their child – fall sick.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Besides the struggles of sourcing suitable caregivers for their children, families often also fret over the financial constraints while striving to provide the best for their children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What is the Government doing to provide stronger support for parents in these areas – particularly when cost of living issues continue to have an adverse impact on this group?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their cuts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our vision for Singapore’s population is: a thriving people, a dynamic economy, an inclusive society and a resilient nation – a Singapore where all Singaporeans can achieve their personal and family aspirations; have good jobs, good incomes and good careers; and live fulfilling lives.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We must also lay the foundations for future generations to do the same.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, we are confronted with the twin demographic challenges of a persistently low fertility rate and an ageing population.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many other advanced societies also face rapidly declining fertility.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: South Korea continues to grapple with a fertility rate below 1.0 – far below the replacement level of 2.1.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Closer to home, Malaysia and Thailand saw their fertility rates fall in 2022.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: European countries, such as Italy and Spain, continue to see record lows in births year on year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the key population outcomes we want and our strategies for achieving them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A strong Singaporean citizenry is the bedrock and wellspring of a thriving nation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We must hence continue to support Singaporeans in starting and raising families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, we must manage the practical impact of slowing local workforce growth and an ageing population on our society and economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is where our immigration, foreign workforce and integration strategies come in.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, we must understand that this task cannot be undertaken by the Government alone.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We can only succeed through our collective efforts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about our population projections and how we plan our population policies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This planning parameter remains relevant for the 2030s.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Beyond that, our population size will depend on various demographic trends, such as birth rates, life expectancies, deaths and migration; as well as future social and economic needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In planning for the longer-term, we develop various scenarios to ensure that we are adequately prepared for a range of possible outcomes, rather than focus on a single number.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In all scenarios, however, supporting marriage and parenthood remains a fundamental priority.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have been and will continue to invest heavily in families as this is an existential issue for us.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Also, our efforts to raise fertility will take time to show results.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A carefully managed immigration policy is hence an important supporting measure to moderate the impact of low birth rates and an ageing population on our society and economy.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, let me now elaborate on our population strategies, the trade-offs we face and the whole-of-society effort needed.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our resident total fertility rate, or TFR, has continued to decline.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are various reasons for Singapore's low fertility.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some are temporal, for instance, couples that had their marriage plans disrupted by COVID-19, which may in turn, have delayed their parenthood plans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Others cite concerns about the financial costs of child-raising, pressures to be an excellent parent, or difficulties managing work and family commitments.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: More broadly though, our low fertility reflects a global phenomenon where individual priorities and societal norms have shifted.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This can be seen from a slew of articles on the TFRs of other countries.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, with your permission, may I please distribute an Annex which has some of these articles, to Members of the House?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What I am circulating is the list, but the articles are accessible there, through the QR code and the links.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These articles reflect a generational change in priorities and how young people around the world are increasingly finding meaning in other pursuits.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They may not even see marriage or parenthood as important life goals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our falling TFR has serious implications for Singapore's future.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are already seeing the impact of our falling TFR on our society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Families today are smaller than before, with more sandwiched couples having to care for both the young and old.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A growing proportion of Singaporeans are remaining single and will have weaker familial support networks when they grow older.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our falling TFR will also impact our economy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As several Members have mentioned, a strong and vibrant economy is critical for Singapore, as it helps raise our standard of living and gives us resources to tackle challenges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, a vibrant economy is ultimately driven by people.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With fewer births, we will face a shrinking workforce.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It will be increasingly challenging to maintain our dynamism, attract global businesses and create opportunities for the next generation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This has been the experience of countries like South Korea and Italy, who are grappling with economic slowdowns and declining wages, further compounded by low fertility and the resulting demographic changes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are therefore determined to address these challenges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The bright side is that our young Singaporeans still aspire towards marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, as several Members have noted, they may not proactively plan towards these goals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As a Government, we respect Singaporeans' personal decisions on marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But there is no denying that starting a family becomes more challenging with age.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Singaporeans may prioritise their education or careers in young adulthood, only to face difficulty conceiving when they eventually try for children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We therefore strongly encourage young Singaporeans to actively build and develop relationships and intentionally factor marriage and parenthood into their life plans early on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Several Members have asked on how we will support marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will provide a conducive environment for couples who wish to start, grow and nurture their families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We made significant moves in this regard at Budget 2023.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To strengthen financial support for young families, we enhanced the Baby Bonus Cash Gift for all birth orders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also enhanced the Child Development Account, or CDA, by increasing the First Step Grant and raising the Government co-matching caps.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are continuing to address the housing needs of Singaporean couples and families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Furthermore, HDB is catching up on BTO projects delayed by the pandemic, having delivered 80% of such projects as of end-2023.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As announced at the National Day Rally last year, the new framework of Standard, Plus and Prime flats will take effect later this year, and cater to Singaporean families' different budgets and needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Ministry of National Development (MND) will help families awaiting the completion of their BTO flats by doubling the supply of flats under the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme, or PPHS, to 4,000 units by 2025.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the meantime, as announced at Budget 2024, MND will also introduce a one-year PPHS (Open Market) Voucher, to support PPHS-eligible families to rent an HDB flat or bedroom from the open market and MND will share more at its COS.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Mr Yip Hon Weng highlighted, some couples may also face fertility issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Couples undergoing Assisted Conception Procedures at our public hospitals can tap on Government co-funding and use their MediSave to offset treatment costs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) is also studying the merits of extending co-funding to the private sector, taking into account clinical outcomes and costs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Based on preliminary data, approximately 200 women underwent elective egg-freezing since it was implemented in June last year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But whilst this may be an available option for women, we still do encourage them to try for children earlier, to reduce age-related risks of conceiving and carrying a baby successfully to term.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling and Ms Hany Soh asked about support to alleviate Singaporeans' concerns regarding child-raising costs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government is investing heavily to ensure preschool, education and healthcare remain affordable for families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, a Singaporean child can receive around $200,000 worth of education subsidies, including preschool subsidies, by the time the child completes secondary school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, of course, there are significant subsidies for studying in the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We had just enhanced the Baby Bonus Scheme last year and will consider the suggestions raised, bearing in mind the overall suite of grants and subsidies available.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, we are also focusing on supporting men in their role as husbands and fathers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Members on both sides of the House support this, and Mr Louis Ng, in particular, has been an active advocate and champion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our leave provisions are differentiated between mothers and fathers to meet their respective needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, maternity leave is longer to allow mothers to recuperate physically from childbirth and to care for and bond with their newborns.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is especially so, as more women want to continue to work while raising their children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, around half of our eligible fathers take paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We encourage more to do so and play a part in caring for your newborns.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Studies have shown that children benefit physically, cognitively and emotionally when their fathers are more involved in parenting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One father, Mr Daniel Lim, looks forward to this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He and his wife have two children and are expecting another in April this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Daniel welcomes the additional paternity leave as it allows him to focus on supporting his wife and caring for his children during this important period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will do so as soon as possible, to benefit more fathers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the meantime, we encourage all employers to start adjusting to ensure a smoother transition when the mandatory provision eventually kicks in.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: During our Forward Singapore engagements, parents shared that care needs are greatest during a child's first 18 months.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to strengthen support for parents during this critical period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MSF has been ramping up infant care capacity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It also plans to grow childminding services as an additional infant care option for families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, we know many Singaporean parents prefer to care for their infants themselves and have asked if more leave can be given.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have studied the leave provisions of other developed countries like France and Denmark which have higher TFRs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These countries tend to provide parents with longer periods of leave during their child's infancy, sometimes at reduced pay.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Parents appreciate the greater peace of mind, as they can care for their infants for longer while remaining employed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We must recognise that this requires workplace adjustments and that employers may face challenges in making arrangements to cover for employees' extended absences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will therefore closely engage tripartite partners on further enhancements and pace out any proposed changes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Caring for and raising our children is a long-term endeavour.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Ms Hany Soh and Miss Rachel Ong have pointed out, this can be especially challenging when children fall sick or for certain groups, such as parents of children with severe disabilities or rare disorders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, beyond leave provisions, we are exploring other sustainable ways to help parents better manage work and family commitments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We must strengthen workplace flexibility in a manner that meets the needs of both employees and employers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Ms Carrie Tan mentioned, we want to provide parents with the flexibility to optimise their energies as they navigate the demands of work and family.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the same time, employers' ability to meet their business needs will be critical in sustaining such flexibility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Through open communication and mutual trust, employers and employees can work out arrangements that meet both their needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) is working with tripartite partners to develop new Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked about Government support for companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We recognise that some employees, including SMEs, may find it more challenging to adopt FWAs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will consider ways to help all employers implement FWAs well and manage their teams productively.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are HR capabilities that will enable our employers to optimise their workforce and position themselves as employers of choice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are glad to see more employers distinguishing themselves by implementing family-friendly practices and features.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One such local company is Hegen, which develops infant care products.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hegen offers its employees various forms of workplace flexibility, including work-from-home arrangements, staggered hours, part-time work and compressed work schedules.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hegen's family-friendly culture has helped the company to attract and retain talent, showing that businesses can pursue excellence and innovation while at the same time implementing family-friendly practices.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We encourage all employers to establish family-friendly workplaces and make a difference in practical ways.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, fathers ought to feel supported when taking time off for their families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A CNA report cited an example of a father who wanted to take paternity leave, but encountered resistance from his female manager.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She made passive-aggressive comments and pointed to the backlog of work he would accumulate if he did so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would have been more helpful to discuss a mutually satisfactory covering arrangement instead.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Employer support can also include family-friendly office features, such as lactation rooms, which Mr Louis Ng spoke about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We encourage building owners to voluntarily provide such family-friendly features beyond the minimum Code requirements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Premises which lack space for separate lactation facilities can consider lactation pods which are commercially available.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: BCA has actively promoted the Fund via press releases, social media posts, industry seminars and targeted engagements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will continue to reach out to building owners to encourage adoption.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But ultimately, it will require a whole-of-society effort to build the family-friendly workplace culture that Members have called for.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All of us have a role to play, whether as parents, employers or co-workers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We want parents to be able to tap on workplace flexibilities without fear of stigma.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Every small act counts, from exercising patience when a colleague’s child interrupts a work call, to being understanding when a co-worker takes time off at short notice to care for their children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also trust that parents will tap on these flexibilities responsibly, and stand ready to reciprocate when other colleagues have urgent personal or family needs to attend to.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Together, we can make Singapore a great place for all to work and live in, for generations to come.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about supporting the needs of an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Indeed, a key thrust of Forward Singapore is enabling our seniors to age well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Primarily, we want our seniors to have good health.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Good health is a lifelong commitment, as lifestyles in earlier years affect how healthy we are in our golden years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Therefore, we will step up the preventive health focus through Healthier SG, to empower Singaporeans to live healthily with support from their regular family doctor.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also want our seniors to age well in their homes and the community.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is the key purpose of Age Well SG, which complements Healthier SG by anchoring ageing well in the community.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Through Age Well SG, we will encourage active ageing, improve support for seniors with care needs, and make our homes and neighbourhoods more senior-friendly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOH, MND and MOT will share more information on their Age Well SG plans during their respective Committee of Supply segments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Gan asked about the number of Migrant Domestic Workers, or MDWs, needed to support our ageing population.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We expect that demand for elderly caregiving services will rise in the coming years, and MDWs play an important role in supporting households with caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, the scale of this increase is uncertain.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It will be dependent on a host of factors, including how well our society ages and other efforts to support seniors with care needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Even as we strive to support Singaporeans in their marriage and parenthood aspirations, and help seniors live healthier and more fulfilling lives, low birth rates and ageing will undeniably impact our economy and society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our immigration policies play an important role in mitigating this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We continue to maintain a measured and stable pace of immigration, which moderates the impact of demographic trends on the size and age profile of the citizen population.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The average number of new citizenships and new PRs granted per year since 2019 is slightly higher than that over the preceding period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We grant PR or citizenship to those who can integrate well, contribute to Singapore and are committed to making Singapore their home.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our immigration policy also helps us to meet our future population needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, in recent years, we have granted a higher number of PRs to healthcare workers to support our growing healthcare needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One such immigrant is Ms Josephine Marie Baljon Celis, who was granted PR in 2023.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She has been a valued staff nurse at SingHealth Community Hospitals for almost 15 years, consistently delivering a high standard of care to her patients.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Josephine’s colleagues describe her as friendly, positive and dedicated to her work.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Beyond her core nursing duties, she has served as a Clinical Instructor for many years, guiding and training numerous batches of nursing students to help meet Singapore’s healthcare needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Like our forefathers, many immigrants have found their way here and stayed on because they hope for a better life in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With time, they become our friends and ultimately, our fellow countrymen who will work alongside us to build a brighter shared future.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But crucial to this brighter shared future is a strong economy, supported by a dynamic and productive workforce.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Mr Patrick Tay, Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Yip Hon Weng have noted, for Singaporeans to have good jobs, good incomes and access to services for a high quality of life, we need a strong economy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our low birth rates and ageing population have resulted in slowing local workforce growth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They can also generate opportunities for Singaporeans by bringing in new investments, networks and expertise.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, even as we welcome these complementary foreign workers, we will continue to strengthen the development of the local workforce.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will also support Singaporeans in gaining overseas work experience to provide opportunities for career development and progression.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: More information will be provided during MTI’s and MOM’s Committee of Supply segments, and we encourage all Singaporeans to make the most of these opportunities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, I have outlined how our marriage and parenthood, immigration and workforce policies work in tandem to help us overcome our population challenges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, these policies can only succeed if we remain an inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Globally, sentiments of disenfranchisement and xenophobia have gained momentum.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A growing number of politicians across the world have stoked xenophobia to gain popular support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some have been voted into office, the result of which has been division and instability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The well-being of Singaporeans remains at the heart of what we do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But this does not prevent us from welcoming foreigners who can contribute to our economy and add richness to our multicultural society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And we must, of course, also work hard at integration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This response extends to the enquiry Mr Faisal Manap made about how we can welcome Malays and others from the region to come and join us.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All that I said earlier about welcoming foreigners here extends to those groups as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in conclusion, Mr Chairman, Singaporeans and their well-being are at the heart of our population strategies.
