speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These strategies aim to build a resilient nation, anchored on the key thrusts of the Forward Singapore Report: opportunities, assurance and collective responsibility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government is committed to building an economy that will provide opportunities for all to achieve their aspirations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government will also provide assurance for Singaporeans at every stage of life.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will not let up on efforts to support Singaporeans in starting and raising families so that we may forge a strong Singaporean citizenry.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For this to happen, we need everyone to do their part.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: I can understand what Ministers have shared earlier on the rationale behind why we want to provide the better subsidy schemes for those who are below 40 years old.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: But through my interactions with several of the residents that have approached me for support and help, I can also understand that, generally, as women, we want to try our best to conceive naturally and without resorting to undergo ACP like IVF, unless circumstances require us to do so.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Several of them, due to factors that are beyond their control, have entered marriage at a later stage and have eventually resorted to trying attempts at IVFs but have failed.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: I do hope that the Government can exercise flexibility in acceding to those appeals for those that have put in the effort and have unfortunately failed two attempts of the IVF trials and, as a result, have sought us to seek support for more additional fundings in order to eventually fulfil their dreams to become a parent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do have a lot of sympathy for those who, for whatever reason, were not able to try for children earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The only thing is that the fact remains that age does remain a factor.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It does affect the success or the outcomes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we can certainly look at it and study it and, as time goes by, if technology gets better, if there are advances and improvements in medical science, then we can see how that can be done.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will do our utmost but, at the same time, just to remember, age is a factor.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, where possible, if we can encourage Singaporeans to have children earlier, that would be really the best solution.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Minister, if I heard right, said that the population projections by 2050 will depend on trends in fertility and longevity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I understand there might be some concerns about publicly revealing population projections but does the Government have any internal projections for the population in 2040 and 2050 based on the different scenarios?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Because in 2013, I recall that the Government was able to project our population until 2030.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Now, in 2024, why is it not possible to project it until at least 2040?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The difference really is that planning for the future has become a lot more complex.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not like when Singapore was first starting off and you have a clear trajectory and you can say that there is this projection.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, having one particular figure does not really help because you would have a range of scenarios.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is what I was trying to explain just now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Essentially, there are birth rates, TFR, we have just seen that it has fallen to an all-time low, life expectancy, deaths, migrations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, basically, for the Ministries to plan, they have to plan on a range of scenarios and not all of them will plan on the same variables.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, if it is public housing, you would just look at Singaporeans, when you plan your BTOs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But, obviously, if you are looking at some other things, then you would take into account the foreigners who work here as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One of the strategies we have for this is modular planning.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for example, if you were building something like T5, you do not have to build the whole thing straightaway to take into account a very large number that is coming through.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You would build stage one and then if it looks like you are having more traffic, then you can build stage two.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We apply some of that when we are planning for public housing, for transport.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, having one particular figure does not really address the issue.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think for the agencies, they are learning over the years, to plan within a range of scenarios.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I think that is important for the fathers, but most important is for the companies, especially for the SMEs, which can then plan ahead and have resources made available in time for when we mandate this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I mean, we do this for carbon tax, where we are given a whole roadmap on when we will increase carbon tax so that companies can get ready.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I hope we can do this also for paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The current rate is at 60%; whether it can increase it to 80%.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Similar for accessible toilets, so that more building owners perhaps will be spurred on to build the lactation rooms and this will help the breastfeeding mothers as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, this is something that we are looking at and the Member can be assured that as and when it does become mandatory, actually when it does become mandatory, it will factor in a lead-in time for the companies as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I thank him for his suggestions with respect to the building code.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Are there any clarifications for Senior Minister Teo?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Earlier on, I did not see any Members raise their hand, so I moved on.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Minister Teo is asking too, whether there are any for him?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in my speech during the Budget Statement debate, I spoke at length about including persons with disabilities (PwDs) and why this is important.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: During the Committee of Supply debates, I will be shifting our focus more towards the "hows" to inclusion.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This raises the issue of fairness and it demands action.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As an illustration: today, individuals with disabilities like Mr A, often encounter insurer assessments that exclude them from total and permanent disability benefits.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In Mr A's case, Asperger's Syndrome and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) had been explicitly cited as reasons for his exclusion when he applied for a whole life insurance policy.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: PwDs who contribute meaningfully to society or hold stable employment, frequently face similar rejections or exclusions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Often, outright denials or vague explanations of underwriting decisions are also given.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This reflects a systemic failure in our insurance industry that disproportionately harms PwDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: There is no transparency in the insurer's decision-making process.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, PwDs are left guessing and are denied the insurance coverage they need and deserve.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we need appropriate measures that mandate insurers to disclose the data, research and methodologies used in the assessments to their customers and regulators, such as MAS and MOH.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This will empower not just PwDs – but all affected Singaporeans – including those with mental health conditions, physical conditions or unrelated illnesses, to challenge unfair decisions and hold insurers accountable.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Where necessary, MAS must also step in to take decisive action against insurers that indiscriminately reject applications – solely based on disability or mental health declarations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Every application must be objectively assessed by the insurer, based on reliable information or data relevant to the risks being insured and auditable.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Clear examples of what is considered discrimination will provide clarity and guidance to insurers to ensure compliance with fair and transparent practices.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The use of irrelevant and discriminatory criteria in risk assessments is a barrier that must be addressed.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Insurers must be prohibited from using factors, such as intelligence quotient (IQ) levels or academic ability, in their underwriting assessments.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Other factors, like sensorimotor skills, must be evaluated judiciously and holistically under strict conditions and only when directly relevant to specific insurance policies and aligned with ethical and regulatory standards.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Unfair or sweeping assessment practices not only perpetuate stigma, but also ignore the diverse experiences and capabilities of PwDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Autistics have shared with me that they feel discriminated against when insurers exclude coverage for certain conditions – especially those related to mental health.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: SG Enable says that autism is a range of conditions – characterised by difficulties in communication and social interaction, sensitivity to sensory stimulation and repetitive behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Autism is not a medical condition, it is a neurological difference.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, even if research shows a high correlation between autism and a particular condition, it is unfair to exclude coverage.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve meaningful change, MAS should take in input from disability organisations and PwDs to refine the guidelines and monitor insurance practices.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Their insights and perspectives are invaluable in ensuring that the needs and rights of PwDs are upheld and protected.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, private insurance is ultimately a business and insurers need to consider the risks presented by each policyholder to charge premiums reflective of the risk.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: However, this does not mean that insurers should be allowed to discriminate against any community in Singapore – including PwDs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, PwDs or special needs often receive inadequate insurance coverage to cover to protect themselves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even if they manage to get insured, the scope of coverage and the insured amounts is often limited.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MAS is proposing to issue guidelines to insurers that they should not indiscriminately reject an application, solely based on a declared personal information subject to disability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister explain when these guidelines will be issued and how they will be materially different or more beneficial to PwDs or special needs?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this, I will raise two points today: developments in Australia and on Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre Ltd (FIDReC).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Importantly, it requires businesses to take all reasonable steps to prevent the misuse of its services by scammers, "so that an undue burden is not placed on consumers to prevent scams." As far as Singapore is concerned, I acknowledge MAS' work, particularly in coming up with the two consultation papers in October on the Shared Responsibility Framework for phishing scams and on the proposed enhancements to the E-payments User Protection Guidelines (EUPG).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, the EUPG paper while imposing some duties on financial institutions, also has a whole section on how consumers should also be subject to enhanced duties – including preventive actions such as updating the browsers of devices and patching operating systems with the latest security updates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How does the MAS assess whether these duties are reasonable, given the wide demographic profile of consumers?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As few customers have the resources to sue their banks in Court, FIDReC is an important low-cost avenue for bank customers to seek redress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Chairman, with your permission, I will be taking clarifications after this reply – if there is available time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Allow me to start first by addressing Mr Ong Hua Han's and Mr Gerald Giam's questions on adopting fair and responsible practices towards PwDs and persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The MAS expects all insurers to deal fairly with their customers, including PwDs and persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Over the past three years, MAS has reinforced these expectations with insurers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: First, MAS has carefully reviewed individual cases that have been highlighted to us to ascertain that customers were treated fairly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Second, MAS has worked with the MSF to consult relevant medical professionals and industry practitioners – to ensure that the underwriting standards of the insurance industry, in particular for PwDs and persons with mental health conditions, are grounded in scientific evidence and data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Third, MAS has also worked with insurers to better explain underwriting outcomes to applicants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The upcoming revision to the MAS Guidelines on Fair Dealing – Board and Senior Management Responsibilities for Delivering Fair Dealing Outcomes to Customers, which Members have raised, formalises all of these expectations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: MAS and MSF have engaged individuals and groups representing PwDs as well as industry practitioners in the process of refining these guidelines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This would fall short of the expectation for insurers to conduct an objective assessment of every application, based on reliable information or data relevant to the risks that are being insured.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This applies to all types of insurance policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In other words, insurers should not reject applications from PwDs and persons with mental health conditions without an assessment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And after they have conducted the detailed assessments, the insurers may choose to accept applications as is, with higher premiums or with specific benefits excluded.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: There may also be instances where the insurers assess the risks to be large and, therefore, are unable to provide coverage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Such cases are unlikely to be unique to Singapore, as insurers typically reference the underwriting guidelines of re-insurers which operate internationally, to which insurers would also transfer some of the risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The reason is that prescribing a "one-size-fits-all" assessment criteria on underwriting would result in some insurers taking on risks that exceed their underwriting expertise and capacity, which will not be prudentially sound.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For example, it could impair access to insurance protection if insurers stop providing coverage under such circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Where the ability of insurers to adjust coverage and premiums for higher-risk individuals is constrained, it could then also lead to higher premiums for policyholders who pose lower risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But I would like to assure the Members that MAS will closely monitor the effective and consistent application and implementation of the revised guidelines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is part of our ongoing supervision of insurers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This will include reviewing the insurers' underwriting policies and processes, including via on-site inspections, to ensure that insurers maintain robust underwriting frameworks that are in line with MAS' regulatory requirements, supervisory expectations and sound international practice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: When an insurer is found to have fallen short, or found to be dealing unfairly with its customers, MAS will take appropriate supervisory actions, such as directing the insurer to review their policies and processes to prevent a recurrence, and to review applications of the affected customers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Individuals who have concerns over their insurer's underwriting decision can make an appeal through their insurer's feedback channel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In this vein, MAS expects insurers to have a robust process to handle customer complaints independently and effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Individuals can also write to MAS, and MAS will investigate accordingly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about efforts to safeguard bank customers' interests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Other Members of Parliament, such as Dr Tan Wu Meng, Dr Lim Wee Kiak, Miss Rachel Ong, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Gerald Giam, have also spoken about this and advocated strongly about this topic in this House.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In her Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) COS speech, Minister of State Sun Xueling will more comprehensively outline the efforts by Government agencies and private sector entities to raise our collective defences against scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These include initiatives and measures that have been explored under the guidance of MAS, such as the banks’ recent anti-malware controls, and the Shared Responsibility Framework (SRF) to strengthen the direct accountability of financial institutions and telcos to consumers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our efforts are bearing fruit, especially for unauthorised transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Despite this progress, we are not resting on our laurels; we will continue to push on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Admittedly, these will add more friction to the banking process, but we acknowledge and understand that these will better safeguard customers’ interests and also reduce the amounts lost through scams in the longer term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Authorised transactions are transactions where victims willingly transfer monies to scammers under social engineering and deception.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We cannot address such scams directly through banking sector-related safeguards alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We must all take steps to protect ourselves, by keeping up with new scam typologies which are rapidly evolving; and also banking controls, and checking for signs of scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have made some collective progress together, but we must and we will continue to strengthen all of these initiatives that I have outlined to help further safeguard bank customers’ interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But even if insurers properly followed all their underwriting principles, many PwDs will still find themselves excluded.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Does the Government have any plans to step in to assist these PwDs who do not have enough coverage?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, we have received feedback on this through Mr Ong Hua Han, Mr Gerald Giam and others who have written directly to us, both at MAS and MOH.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we are doing a few things to ensure that overall, both insurers and the applicants are able to understand what PwDs and persons with mental health conditions require, and their circumstances.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, let me enumerate a few different aspects, so that it is rather comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In this regard, MSF, partners such as the Autism Resource Centre, the Life Insurance Association and us have embarked in the following efforts – and I hope that the Members can also support us in these efforts.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, it is important to further enhance the awareness and understanding on PwDs and the various support systems in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is to enable insurers themselves to better take into account all of these different factors in their underwriting.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The second is to provide further training on communications with PwDs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Third, to raise an overall awareness on health underwriting among consumers, including PwDs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Fourth, we are working on this – to explore initiatives to further improve the insurance application process.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I think we are in line with international best practices.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But it is an iterative process, it is an evolving process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have two broad clarifications for the Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: During his response he mentioned several times about closely the MAS is working with banks to come up with guidelines, preventive measures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But he did not say anything about how MAS was working with consumers at all, before the draft guidelines are issued.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: For instance, like I mentioned in my cut, the EUPG paper that sets out the enhanced duties of consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Were any consumers consulted about whether these duties are reasonable before the draft guidelines came out?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, the first clarification is about how MAS works with consumers, if at all, before it comes up with such guidelines in this area.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I think he would have noticed from what was being proposed by the Australian Treasury was that actually there would be a consumer protection body at the top of the apex when it came to looking at consumer interests in the scam space.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This body actually has an overarching responsibility that cuts across sectors – banking, telcos, digital platforms – all that would sort of come under that consumer protection umbrella and there is going to be legislation, I believe, intended for this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I find that in Singapore, this is missing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: There is no consumer protection overarching body that seems to be looking across the different industry sectors on whether consumers are getting a fair deal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I wonder if he can comment on whether he thinks that such a body would actually add value to our interest in protecting consumers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Maybe I will just add, on the EUPG first.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The EUPG, as you compared to the Australia's E-Payments Code; there is a list of consumer duties within the EUPG, as the Member had mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And these are cyber hygiene duties that the consumer ought to perform.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And that is why as a whole, I think that is very, very important, not just for duties by banks, telcos; but also in order to address scams, the consumers need to play an important role.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They are also in line with public education efforts that the Government has been reinforcing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We also expect banks to treat customers fairly and take into account the specifics of the scams and the profile of the victims.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are assessing this feedback on both in SRF as well as EUPG, and in many of the different consultations, we reach out to consumers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The second on the SRF, the topic about the Australian example is the Scams Code Framework.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Scams Code Framework is quite similar to our SRF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In the same way, it also looks at duties by financial institutions as well as telcos.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think the Australian example has other sectors as well that are inputted into this.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We had mentioned in the SRF that we will continue to review it and see how these duties can be applied and where possible and where it is appropriate, we are looking at different countries' experiences with it and we may expand it.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will review and it will evolve over time.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But I would also like to share with the Member that the experiences in different countries are also very different.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The way that the banks, the telcos, operators and other aspects within the ecosystem that deal with this issue is also very different.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I want to assure her and I assure the Members that we continue to take all of these into account.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we will continue to review them over time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Lim, I will come back to you because I just want to clear the rest of the cuts, and if we have time, I will come back to you.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The plethora and spectrum of issues confronting the Public Service are becoming more complex and cut across agencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: For example, COVID-19 showed that public health pandemic had implications on many other aspects such as the economy, education, work, social connections and support.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Beyond COVID-19, we also see families with more complex needs cutting across multiple areas such as jobs, healthcare, education, emotional support and financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We are also seeing major changes on other fronts such as geopolitics, generative AI and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: To tackle challenges ahead that are becoming more complex, the Public Service must review and refresh its agenda.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: To help develop and deliver this, public officers must also build new skills and experiences to better understand changing citizen needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Public officers also need to understand changing external forces as geopolitics become more complex and even issues like sustainability have global dimensions and ramifications.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Generative AI has also morphed the way we can and should do things ethically and without compromising data security and confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, as Singapore navigates an increasingly complex future, our residents' needs will grow even more diverse and interconnected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: We must shift from agency-centric services to citizen-centric ones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: We can no longer expect Singaporeans to navigate bureaucratic silos, going from agency to agency to access essential assistance for multiple needs which are in fact interconnected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Imagine a scenario where families in need seamlessly access financial aid, job training, housing assistance and healthcare for seniors, all through a single, integrated platform.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: This holistic approach, where services revolve around residents rather than agencies, is not just a vision but a necessity today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Initiatives like ServiceSG and the Municipal Services Office have made strides towards service integration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Minister also share the Government's broader roadmap for further integrating and streamlining citizens’ access to services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: While digitalisation holds immense potential and we should continue to pursue this as much as possible, physical accessibility remains critical for those who need it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Minister share plans to expand dedicated physical service counters for seniors and individuals lacking digital literacy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Minister also elaborate on the existing mechanisms for escalation across agencies, and how timely resolution is ensured?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: What are the types of cases that usually fall through the cracks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How is the Ministry addressing such cases to ensure no citizens are left behind?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is important to maintain and enhance this relationship.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, ties between state and society do not exist in a vacuum.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As Singapore becomes an ever more important commercial and financial hub, more money and interests will flow into Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They will have interests to advance and protect.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It may involve the appointment of sitting Members of Parliament to boards or the hiring of former Members of Parliament and senior public servants to advise on the shaping of policy and legislation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We often see events by industry associations and others attended by elected officials.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet what is important is how a system regulates lobbying to ensure that the proper political process is not circumvented, and there is no undue disadvantage given to different groups in society, especially those with less money, access and voice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To this end, how can we improve oversight on lobbying activities given Singapore’s changing circumstances?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some of this information is already provided by political parties under legislation governing political donations and the recently enacted Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act, or FICA.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some will say that such a move is not foolproof.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The perfect cannot become an enemy of the good.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Properly regulating lobbying activity and addressing potential conflicts of interest reduces chances of excessive influence by certain groups and a shorting of political processes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is an improvement on the current absence of formal regulation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some may find allowing more public scrutiny onerous.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Building public trust in increasingly complex situations also comes with those in positions of authority trusting the public, not just calling on the public to trust authority.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This not only must be done but must be seen to be done.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Incorruptibility is fundamental to the success of the Singapore Government.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As described in the Code of Conduct, this would help counter potential allegations of corruption and unexplained wealth, and to avoid potential conflicts between private interests and public responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Public declarations would thus go a long way in ensuring public accountability, the Singaporeans to whom the executive serves, and not just accountability to the President.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps we can consider adopting such a practice in Singapore as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such declarations would go some way to bridge the trust gap between Singaporeans and their elected officials, and also help to prevent the spread of misinformation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For a start, we need not make the full disclosures of sensitive details mandatory.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, in the case of residential properties, unit numbers can be redacted to protect the privacy of the Minister involved.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure that this practice will be appreciated by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The question of whether our Ministers can be trusted to scrupulously avoid any actual or apparent conflict of interest between their official duties and private financial interests, as the Ministers' Code of Conduct requires them to do, has been raised before in this house.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: During a Parliamentary Session on the rental of 26 Ridout Road last year, People's Action Party Member of Parliament Poh Li San suggested that it would be in the interest of transparency for Minister Shanmugam and Minister Vivian to declare all their property assets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, this was not a requirement under the Code of Conduct at the time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, we are currently operating in an increasingly hostile global environment – one that is marked by fear, uncertainty and doubt.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For Singapore to successfully navigate ourselves through these uncertain waters, we must ensure that our Public Service officers have broad perspectives so that they are equipped to take on the challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Does PSD plan to allow more of its officers to go on such secondments?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond secondments to private sector and civil society, we should also groom officers to better appreciate international viewpoints and equip them with the ability to negotiate globally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Does PSD offer structured programmes for public sector officers to take on attachments at international and regional organisations?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the PSD will provide officers with a structured framework for rotation outside of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will allow future Public Service leaders to better understand the private sector, social sector and the international domain, and factor these perspectives when conceptualising and implementing policies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, the global environment is becoming increasingly challenging and susceptible to rapid change.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a country, we also have matured and are now in transition.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To imagine and chart our future as a nation will require greater engagement and partnership between the Government and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For one, the Government does not have a monopoly on the best ideas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Further, the Government's aim is to serve our citizens and closer engagement is necessary to better gauge citizens' trust and satisfaction in public services and institutions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The recent Forward SG exercise, launched in June 2022 to engage Singaporeans from all walks of life, has laid out a new social compact for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To move towards this new compact, changes are expected to be made in both Government policies and the way the Government engages and partners Singaporeans in creating and delivering policies and programmes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a welcome move to strengthen partnerships between the Government, private and people sectors for the national good.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The new organisation could become the first stop for people to share ideas or proposals, gather other like-minded individuals and organisations, and access opportunities for citizen-government collaborations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond the formation of the SGPO, may I ask how is the Public Service reorganising itself to better serve citizens and public good amid a changing environment and more frequent volatility?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can we better set ourselves up to tackle increasingly complex external forces and growing interdependency of issues as well as the build-up of complex domestic matters.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, many officers who join the Public Service are driven by the higher purpose of doing good, wanting to serve and make a difference to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Public officers can do good both through their, or during their work, or outside of work, fostering a culture of civic and engagement and social responsibility.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It helps foster volunteerism amongst public officers and also improves their understanding of ground issues.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, if properly matched, their voluntary services will enrich their beneficiaries with valuable manpower and skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have personally had the opportunity to serve with several senior public officers like Permanent Secretary Teo Zsin Woon and Deputy Secretary Poon Hon Yuen in the disability and the seniors space in initiatives beyond their day jobs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Recently, I also heard that public officers across the Service signed up as befrienders to seniors who live alone in Marine Parade.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chairman, we thank all the Members for their cuts, questions and suggestions for the Public Service and how we can do better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Indeed, today we have a Public Service that the vast majority, if not all Singaporeans, can be proud of.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But we, in the Public Service, we are acutely aware of the need for us to stay ahead of the game.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As Mr Patrick Tay mentioned, technology is changing rapidly.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The way countries are organising themselves and their Public Service are also rapidly evolving.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must be careful that we do not rest on our laurels.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We continue to innovate, continue to want to do better and come up with new solutions, lest we be overtaken by others.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And if we do not have a strong, committed and innovative Public Service, it will certainly not help us to inspire confidence in investors, local enterprises, to put their investments here to create good jobs for our people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, our Government believes that we cannot rely on today's or yesterday's solutions for tomorrow's problem.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have to constantly look for new processes, new organisations, to meet tomorrow's challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A forward-looking and future-ready Public Service is central to Singapore's success.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Increasingly, our Public Service will be organised in a much more mission-centric way, given the complexity and interdependency of issues that many Members have mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This has worked out well and borne fruit.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: NCCS has allowed us to sharpen our focus on climate change issues across the whole of Government, cutting across many agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, NCCS worked with MSE to develop the Singapore Green Plan 2030 to achieve our long-term goal of net zero emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But behind that, there was participation from MTI, MOE, MOM and many other agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are seeing the fruits of this effort too.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, robots are increasingly deployed in buildings for services like cleaning and security, but they cannot communicate with each other because of different manufacturers having their own proprietary software.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To drive the adoption of robotics and automation, S&TPPO worked with A*STAR and GovTech to adapt and deploy a universal middleware for the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: With this, robots from different manufacturers can now communicate with one another and with lifts, doors and security gantries to move autonomously around buildings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Successful trials have been completed in the Tampines Regional Library and the JTC Summit with the National Library Board (NLB) and JTC.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: S&TPPO is working with GovTech and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) to further test the product with other public and private sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Yet another example where they have become much more mission-focused, mission-centric is ground operations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To improve efficiency, S&TPPO and GovTech are working with agencies to apply video analytics rather than just focusing on each agency's own CCTV video feed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: S&TPPO is driving the consolidation of these sensitive feeds into a cloud video exchange before applying video analytics to the consolidated video feeds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This can improve decision-making and respond times, such as identifying an overcrowding situation that requires intervention or preventing worksite incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to build on these successes to refine the way we organise ourselves going forward.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In response to Ms Mariam Jaafar's earlier questions to Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong about centralisation, from a Public Service perspective, we just want to say this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Centralisation is not the only way that we can allow better coordination across the various agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In fact, depending on the nature of the problem, we have different methods.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Sometimes, we may start up a new agency, centralise and put it under the PMO to incubate it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: At other times, we may assign one of the agencies to be, if you like, the lead or the first among equals to coordinate that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But that agency, that lead agency, is, if you like, a mini joint staff.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It must have people participating from other agencies to support it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our hope is that over time, each and every one of our agencies, when tackling a new problem, can be a mini joint staff where it can harness the energies and capabilities and capacities of other agencies to come together.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, it does not mean that every new problem that requires more coordination needs to be centralised at the PMO or to create a new agency.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, let me respond to Mr Yip Hong Weng's questions on how we reorganise our service delivery for us to be much more citizen-centric.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the digital sphere, we have made great strides in making services more intuitive, seamless and relevant for our citizens, and we will continue to improve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A key feature is the Care Services Recommender for caregivers to find the support they need easily and conveniently.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Another example is MyLegacy@LifeSG portal, which helps citizens plan ahead for end-of-life matters.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Even as more services are digitised, the Public Service is committed to ensuring that our services continue to be accessible and inclusive for all.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Seniors who have difficulty making online transactions can simply walk in.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Officers are cross-trained to help them access frequently used digital services.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And 70% of citizens visiting ServiceSG centres in 2023 were aged 55 and above.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to expand the network of ServiceSG centres to prioritise areas with higher demand and concentration of citizens, particularly seniors, who require support with multiple digital transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are whole-of-Government service standards to ensure agencies uphold a consistent and satisfactory level of service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To avoid cases falling through the cracks, we have a no-wrong-door policy for any public feedback received.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to ensure that our policies, standards and practices are inclusive to all.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For municipal services, the Municipal Services Office (MSO), coordinates across agencies and Town Councils to serve residents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For businesses, MTI and GovTech are continuously evolving the Go Business portal to facilitate a globally competitive, pro-enterprise operating environment in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Go Business portal allows businesses to access services across multiple Government agencies by milestone movements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, these are just examples of how the Public Service is organising and evolving our organisation to be much more mission-centric and much more citizen-centric.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Within the Service, public officers can gain new skill sets from formal training courses and increasingly through hands-on development opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These range from short-term attachments, what we call Short-term Immersion Programmes (STIP) or gig work, to longer-term job rotations or structured job rotations (SJR).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Just as an example – Service SG Centre Head, Ms Uma, signed up for STIP with the Agency for Integrated Care's (AIC's) Silver Generation Office.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: She engaged seniors to better understand their concerns and share how Government can support them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are happy to report that the people who have gone through this programme have found the cross-pollination of ideas very useful and at the same time it helps them to build the network of relationships required for a much more responsive Government service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are also deliberate in exploring alternative modalities such as boot camps and competitions to generate interest in building new capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To build data capabilities, GovTech organises the annual Data Champions Boot Camp and Data Arcade Tournament.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To build AI capabilities, GovTech launched a Prom Royale Award, a Prom Engineering Competition last year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This year, GovTech will launch a new AI Champions Boot Camp.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Public officers can also expand their perspectives through exposure beyond the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are encouraging the public officers to experience the perspective of citizens and businesses through stints in the private and people sectors, such as the Talent Attachment Programme (TAP).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Under the TAP, Enterprise SG officers like Clarence Tan was attached to DBS Bank's business analytics team.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There, he learned how to operate with big commercial data sets to achieve an all-round understanding of customers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, Ivy Lee from NLB volunteered with Friends-in-deed Counselling Society as a certified counsellor.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In her journey with three individuals over 10 months, she deepened her empathy and communication skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This helped her to become a more empathetic middle manager in NLB.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: An effective Public Service needs to operate well, both locally and internationally.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are equipping more public officers with broader international perspective through exchange programmes and deployment to international organisations at all levels where they fly the Singapore flag high.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Just to give some examples, Ambassador Rena Lee, who is the current CEO of IPOS, was elected as President of the Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In 2018, when she was an officer in Attorney-General's Chambers' (AGC's) International Affairs Division.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As IGC President, Rena built upon her strong international networks and mastery of international law, which helped her build bridges during multilateral negotiations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The success of Ambassador Lee's presidency has entrenched Singapore's standing in the international community as a top leader in international law and as an advocate for a rules-based multilateral system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Another example, Mr Daryl Ong from the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) participated in a two-year Madrid Fellowship Programme administered by the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Through this, he built his network with other countries' trademark examiners and deepened his knowledge of the Madrid Protocol.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Daryl transformed the way trademark data is communicated from IPOS to WIPO to be faster and more accurate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to look out for opportunities for our officers to be attached to international organisations at all levels, including the UN agencies, because this allows us to understand what are the issues that are evolving at the international circles and how we can better prepare ourselves to integrate and work with these agencies in time to come.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond organising ourselves differently and building new capabilities in our offices, we also need to partner differently.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As part of Forward SG, partnership is a key component of the refreshed social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service has worked hard over generations to earn the trust of Singaporeans and is committed to a strong system of governance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms He Ting Ru asked whether our regulations or practices need any updates to ensure that our governance frameworks are not compromised and Mr Louis Chua asked about making assets declarations public for Ministers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I think I have responded to these topics previously, extensively in past Parliamentary replies, but if I may, I will just reiterate a few things.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I think different countries have different rules for their people and organisations and as all of us will agree, no one rule is a panacea to prevent corruption or lobbying.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But what we need to do is to look at the system holistically.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: What we also need to do is to look at the outcome that we have achieved and ask ourselves what is the scale and magnitude of our problem.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Putting in new and more rules does not necessarily solve the problems that we may not even have to start with.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Whenever we put in new rules, we must also be careful if it causes any unintended consequences.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, I just checked the data that was quoted by some Members about some of the countries that have perhaps adopted some of those rules.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, the UK was ranked somewhere between 11 and 20.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, I think when we look at how to make sure that we retain the trust of our people, we must look at it at a system level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If I may reiterate what I have said previously, this must occur at three levels.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, we must make sure that we select good people with the right values to understand not just the letter of the law, but the spirit of the law and uphold them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, we must work as a system, as a team, to make sure that we look out for one another, check one another's blind spots, help to prevent one another from falling into a situation where they might be compromised.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And third, we must have layers of checks internally and externally to pick up issues whenever there are problems.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: That is how we have managed to keep our system relatively corruption-free, lobby-free all these years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But we will be the first to admit that no system is perfect and the situation is evolving and every time we put in rules, there will be parties out there that will try to go around our rules and we have to keep constantly evolving our own rules to make sure that we are never complacent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In trying to copy other people's rules, we must see what they have been able to achieve versus what we have been able to achieve, what problems they have been able to solve versus what problems we are trying to solve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And we should also have a care for the confidentiality of the information, the privacy concerns of the senior officers in the Public Service, including the political office holders.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I think for every rule that we put in, there are implications that we should consider carefully and ask ourselves whether the price that we pay is commensurate with the problem that we are trying to solve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked how the Government can partner citizens better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond partnering on issues that are already on the national agenda, we will engage citizens to set the agenda.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are building from a position of strength.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have already established a clear track record of engagements and partnerships with the community from consulting to co-creating and co-delivering solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For lower-income families and their children, we have moved beyond public consultations on Government proposals to proactively co-create and co-deliver solutions with the public.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, under the Growing Together with KidSTART initiative, corporates and volunteers partnered KidSTART Singapore to co-create fun learning opportunities for KidSTART families and their children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As part of the Singapore Green Plan 2030, the Green Action for Community (GAC) movement was launched in 2022 to involve the community in co-creating ground-up sustainability efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are also strengthening partnerships with the private sector.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: During COVID-19, many came forward to help and co-create solutions together with the government.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are also formalising our partnerships with corporates, such as the MOU with Singapore Airlines last month, to collaborate in areas such as training and volunteer management in essential support care roles in the healthcare sector and this will also allow the Public Service to search our capabilities in the contingencies, drawing upon some of the capacities in the private sector.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I launched it in July last year to provide public officers with opportunities to actively partner citizens on a personal level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Having said that, I come back to where I started.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Past success is no guarantee for future success.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I have shared how we are going to evolve the way we operate, develop our capabilities and partner others for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must look ahead and continue to plan ahead, even if it means disrupting ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In fact, we rather disrupt ourselves before other people disrupt us, so that our Public Service can continue to transform and remain relevant to the future needs of Singapore, and it will be a Public Service where all Singaporeans can be proud of.
